To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

patients who had high occupational status at the start of treatment and who had higher work ability at treatment end were more likely to return to work 6 months after treatment end, compared to patients who did not.

patients who have a low occupational status, low work ability and negative expectations about future work ability at the time of treatment completion have a higher risk of remaining on sick leave 6 months after treatment.

occupational status and work ability at the start of the treatment, and the expectancy of future return to work, are important predictors of long-term return to work in patients with common mental disorders.

the identification of factors that predict RTWs after treatment of common mental disorders.
the identification of factors that can be used in the clinical setting to predict long-term disability in patients with CMDs.
how the individual's perception of the future and his or her own abilities can be used as predictors for RTW.

the predictors of return to work are high occupational status and high work ability at the time of treatment.
a positive expectancy of future workability is associated with a successful return to work.

patients with CMDs who have high occupational status and a positive expectancy of future workability have a better chance to return to work after treatment.
the more the patient feels able to work and the more they expect to work, the more likely they are to return to work.

the expectancy of future ability to work should be included in the assessment of work disability in patients with CMDs, as this is an important predictor of RTW.
